sections.title: 1. Purpose and place in the outline

blocks.text: The Workshop is one of the two practical-arts tracks (§6): the competencies of maintaining a house, a property, and the things that break. Its through-line, in the outline's words, is that a man should be the one who knows what to do when something goes wrong.

In Grade 3 the child moves from watching to doing: real hand tools, under direct supervision (§6, grade phasing for Grades 2–3). Grade 3 also adds two new courses to the track: Home Repair and Maintenance and Fire, Knife and Rope (§5, Grade 3).
Enrollment. The outline presents the Workshop to boys and the Hearth to girls by default, and any family may choose either track, or both, without friction or explanation (§6).

blocks.text: The outline's grade phasing is the rule (§6):
Real hand tools, always with an adult watching. The adult is within arm's reach for saws, knives and fire.
No power tools in Grade 3. The first power tool, a drill with an adult present, comes in Grade 4. No blade-bearing power tool before Grade 6.
Safety glasses for sawing, hammering and drilling; work gloves for heavy work.
Knife rules (Term 4): cut away from the body; keep a "blood circle" (arm's length) clear; close or sheathe the knife when not cutting; hand it over handle first.
Fire rules (Term 5): only with an adult; a bucket of water and a shovel ready; a cleared ring of ground; never leave a fire; drown it, stir it, feel it cold.
Gas, electricity and the breaker box are shown, not handled. The adult operates them.
Practical arts aren't graded.
Skills checklist each term: can the child do the term's skills safely and confidently?
Project log: a photo or drawing of each project, with a sentence about how it was made. It goes in the portfolio.
The year's first repair (Term 6) is written up from problem to fix: the start of the Grade 5 culminating work, a documented home repair (§6).

blocks.text: Projects carry over freely. A missed week just moves the project along.
Weather: Terms 3 and 4 work indoors; Term 5's fire can wait for a dry, still day.
Never rush a tool skill to catch up. Safety comes before schedule.

A child's toolbox: a 13-ounce claw hammer · a small hand saw and a miter box · a tape measure and a try square · a pencil · screwdrivers (flat and Phillips) · pliers · a hand drill ("egg-beater" style) and bits · sandpaper and a block · safety glasses and work gloves · a plunger · rope (about 20 feet of 1/4-inch) and light cord for lashing · bar soap and a vegetable peeler or carving tool for soap carving · a folding or fixed-blade carving knife suitable for a child, used only with an adult. Each term manual lists anything more.

terms.title: Early Autumn · Hand Tools and Shop Safety

head: Strand
Hand Tools and Shop Safety (§6)
rows: Skills
Shop rules and tool names · measuring and marking · hammering · sawing in a miter box · sanding and screwdriving · tool care
Project
A tool caddy to carry the child's own tools all year
Courtesy of the term
Holding the door for others
Tasks
A skill · B real work (2 a week × 6 = 12)

reference.title: Shop rules (teach in week 1, post on the wall)

blocks.text: 1. An adult is in the shop whenever tools are out.
2. Safety glasses on for hammering, sawing and drilling.
3. Every tool has a home, and goes back there.
4. Carry tools pointing down; never run with a tool.
5. Clamp the work, not your hand.
6. Clean up before you leave.

reference.title: Courtesy of the term: holding the door

blocks.text: Each day, hold the door for whoever comes behind, especially someone carrying something, and an older person. At week 6, ask: who did you hold the door for?

Shop rules and tool names. Go through the six rules. Then name each tool and what it's for: claw hammer (drives and pulls nails), hand saw (cuts wood), tape measure and square (measure and mark straight lines), screwdrivers (flat and Phillips), pliers (grip and hold), hand drill (makes holes). Put on safety glasses and check they fit.
Set up a work spot: a sturdy table or bench, a clamp, a place for each tool (a box, a shelf or a pegboard with outlines drawn). Practice the clean-up routine: sweep, tools home, glasses away.

Measuring and marking. Hook the tape on the end of the board and read the inches. The long marks are inches; the shorter ones are halves and quarters. Mark with a sharp pencil, using a small V pointing to the exact spot. Then lay the square against the board's edge and draw a straight line across through the V. (Arithmetic: inches and feet, Term 2.)
On scrap boards, mark and square lines at 3, 6, 8½ and 12 inches. Check each with the tape.

Hammering. Hold the hammer near the end of the handle, not the head. Start the nail with light taps, holding it with pliers or a clothespin so fingers stay clear. Then firm, steady blows, eyes on the nail. To pull a bent nail, slide the claw under the head and rock the handle back.
A nail board: drive ten nails into a scrap block, then pull two out with the claw.

Sawing in a miter box. The box holds the saw straight. Clamp the board in place. Line the saw up on the waste side of the pencil line, start with a few gentle back strokes, then use long, steady strokes and let the saw do the work. Support the off-cut so it doesn't snap.
Cut the caddy pieces (see the cut list below). The adult marks and checks; the child saws.

Sanding and screwdriving. Wrap sandpaper around a block and sand with the grain, never across it, until edges are smooth. Then the screwdriver: the right size tip, push in firmly while turning ("righty-tighty, lefty-loosey").
Assemble the caddy with nails: the adult holds the pieces square while the child nails. Sand any rough edges.
Tool care: wipe tools clean; a drop of oil on the saw blade and the hammer head; check handles are tight; store every tool in its home. Then the skills checklist (below).
Finish the caddy and fill it with the child's own tools. Write the project log page.
From pine boards from a hardware store (ask for them to be cut roughly to length if you like):

blocks.text: Use any simple one-board birdhouse plan (many are free online and in library books), made from a single 1×6 pine board about 5 feet long. For wrens and chickadees, the entrance hole is 1⅛ inches, set about 6 inches above the floor. A plan with a side that swings open lets the house be cleaned each year.
Angled cuts (for a sloped roof) are made by the adult; the child makes the straight cuts.

reference.title: Courtesy of the term: carrying the heavy thing

blocks.text: Each day, offer to carry the heavy bag, the box, the basket of laundry, the groceries from the car. Say "Let me take that." At week 12, ask: what heavy thing did you carry?
Reading a plan. Look at the drawing together: each piece has a name and a size. Read the cut list aloud. Count the pieces. Ask: which pieces are the same size?

Mark every piece on the board, end to end, with the tape and square, labeling each one in pencil (FRONT, BACK, FLOOR…). The adult checks before any cutting. (Arithmetic: adding the lengths to see they fit the board.)

Sawing to a line without a miter box. Clamp the board to the bench with the line just past the edge. Start the cut on the waste side with a few back strokes, then keep the saw upright and watch the line.
Cut the straight pieces. The adult cuts any angled ones. Sand the cut ends.

Drilling with a hand drill. Mark the spot with a nail tap so the bit doesn't wander. Hold the drill upright, turn the handle steadily, and let the bit do the work. Put scrap wood underneath so the bit doesn't split the back.
Drill four small drainage holes in the floor and two small air holes near the top of the sides. The adult drills the 1⅛-inch entrance hole (with a hand brace and bit, or a power drill: adult only).

Nailing a corner. Hold two boards at a right angle, against a square or in a corner clamp. Start the nails in the top board first, then drive them into the edge of the other. A slight angle holds better.
Assemble the back, floor and one side, the adult holding pieces square while the child nails.
A side that swings open. Two nails, one near the top of each edge, act as hinges so the side can pivot for cleaning; a nail or screw near the bottom holds it shut.
Attach the swinging side, the front and the roof. Sand everything smooth. Leave the inside unpainted; the outside can be left natural or painted a light color.
Where to hang it: 5 to 10 feet up, on a post or tree, with the hole facing away from the strongest winds and out of full afternoon sun. Then the skills checklist (below).

Hang the birdhouse with an adult on the ladder. Watch it over the winter and into spring. (Fine Arts studies Audubon's birds in Term 5; the nature journal can follow any birds that move in.) Write the project log page.

One board, many lessons. Measuring, sawing, drilling and nailing all come together this term. Expect it to take the whole six weeks.

head: Strand
Home Repair and Maintenance (§6), new in Grade 3
rows: Skills
The water shutoffs · where the gas and electricity come in · bulbs, batteries and smoke alarms · the furnace filter · the plunger and drain care · how a faucet washer works
Project
A "where things are" map of the house, and a maintenance walk-round with a parent
Courtesy of the term
Giving up your seat
Tasks
A skill · B real work (2 a week × 6 = 12)

glance.text: Indoor term. Everything this term is done inside the house, which suits the winter.
Look, don't touch applies to gas and electricity. The child learns where they are and what to do in an emergency: fetch an adult. The adult operates them.

reference.title: Courtesy of the term: giving up your seat

blocks.text: Each day, stand up and offer your seat to an adult or an older person who comes into the room, at home, in church or on a bus. At week 18, ask: whom did you give your seat to?

The water shutoffs. Find the main water shutoff together (often where the water pipe enters the house, in a basement, crawl space or utility room). Then the small valves under the kitchen and bathroom sinks and behind the toilet. With an adult, turn an under-sink valve off (clockwise), check the tap, and turn it back on. Why it matters: a burst pipe or a leak is stopped by turning off the water.
Start the house map: draw a simple plan of the house and mark the main water shutoff and each sink and toilet valve.

Gas and electricity: where, not how. Find the gas meter and shutoff (if the house has gas) and the breaker box or fuse box. Read the labels on the breakers together. The rules: if you smell gas, leave the house and tell an adult at once; never touch the breaker box or a fuse; never touch an outlet with wet hands.
Add them to the map, and make a small safety rules card to keep with it.

Bulbs, batteries and smoke alarms. To change a bulb: switch off, let the old bulb cool, twist it out counterclockwise, twist the new one in until snug. To change a battery: match the + and − marks. Test a smoke alarm with its test button, with an adult.
Do the rounds: replace a burned-out bulb, change the batteries in a flashlight or remote, and test every smoke alarm in the house with an adult. Mark the smoke alarms on the map.
The furnace or air filter. Find it with an adult. Read the size printed on the edge, and find the arrow that shows which way the air flows. A dirty filter makes the furnace work harder.
Replace the filter with an adult (furnace off first), arrow pointing the right way. Write the date on the new filter's edge, and mark the filter on the map.

The plunger and drain care. A cup plunger is for sinks; a flange plunger (with the extra lip) is for toilets. Cover the drain completely, then push and pull steadily to loosen a clog. Keeping drains clear: clean the hair and food out of strainers before it builds up.
Clean every drain strainer in the house, and practice plunging a sink with a little water in it.

weeks.title: How a faucet works; the walk-round

blocks.text: How a faucet washer works. Look at an old faucet, a hardware-store display, or a picture: a small rubber washer presses against a seat to stop the water. When it wears out, the faucet drips. Replacing it is a repair for later grades, or for the adult with the child watching. Then the skills checklist (below).
The maintenance walk-round: go through the house with the map and a parent, checking each place on it. Note anything that needs fixing for Term 6's first repair. Write the project log page.

The map is worth keeping on the refrigerator or by the main shutoff. Children who know where the water shutoff is have helped stop floods.
Be calm about gas and electricity. The goal is a child who knows what to do (get an adult, leave if you smell gas), not one who is frightened.

terms.title: Late Winter · Fire, Knife and Rope I: Knots, Lashings and the Knife

head: Strand
Fire, Knife and Rope (§6), new in Grade 3: this term, rope and the knife; fire comes in Term 5
rows: Skills
Square knot · two half hitches · clove hitch · bowline · square lashing · tripod lashing · knife rules · soap carving
Project
A lashed tripod (a camp stand or a flagpole stand) and a soap carving
Courtesy of the term

glance.text: Indoor-friendly. Knots and lashings can be practiced at the kitchen table on a cold day; the tripod can be lashed in a garage.

reference.title: Knife rules (teach in week 23, before any carving)

blocks.text: 1. A knife is used only with an adult present, sitting down.
2. Cut away from your body and your other hand, always.
3. Keep a "blood circle" clear: hold out your arm with the closed knife and turn around. No one should be inside that circle.
4. Close or sheathe the knife whenever you're not cutting.
5. Pass it handle first, closed, and say "Thank you" when you take it.
6. A sharp knife is safer than a dull one; it cuts where you aim it. The adult keeps it sharp.

reference.title: Courtesy of the term: noticing who needs help

blocks.text: Each day, look around: who is carrying too much, can't reach something, is struggling with a door or a coat? Help before you're asked. At week 24, ask: who did you notice?
The square knot. For tying two ends together around something: "right over left, then left over right." Check it lies flat; a granny knot (both the same way) slips.
Tie up bundles: newspapers for recycling, kindling sticks, a bundle of garden stakes. (Literature's fable The Bundle of Sticks in Term 3: a bundle tied together is strong.)

Two half hitches and the clove hitch. Two half hitches tie a rope to a post or a ring: around the post, then two loops around the rope itself. The clove hitch starts a lashing: two loops around a pole, the second crossing over the first and tucked under.
Put up a line between two posts or trees with two half hitches at each end: a clothesline or a line to hang a tarp.
The bowline, a loop that won't slip or tighten. Make a small loop in the rope (the "hole"); then "the rabbit comes up out of the hole, runs around the tree, and goes back down the hole." Pull tight.
Use the bowline: tie a loop to hang a bucket from a branch or a hook, and test it with some weight.

The square lashing, which joins two poles at a right angle. Clove hitch on the upright pole just under the crosspiece; wrap three or four times around both, going over the crosspiece and behind the upright; then two or three tight frapping turns between the poles; finish with a clove hitch on the crosspiece.
Lash two sticks into a cross, then two more crosses, and join them into a small frame.

Knife rules (above), taught carefully and said back by the child. Then soap carving: a bar of soap is soft and forgiving. Use a vegetable peeler or a blunt knife to scrape and carve, always away from the body.
Carve a simple shape from a bar of soap: a fish, a boat, a turtle. Draw the outline on the soap first, then scrape away everything outside it.

The tripod lashing. Lay three poles side by side. Clove hitch on an outside pole; weave the rope over and under the three poles five or six times, loosely; frap between the poles; finish with a clove hitch. Stand the poles up and spread the legs. Then the skills checklist (below).
Build a lashed tripod from three straight poles or garden stakes, about 4 to 6 feet: a stand for a water bucket, a flagpole, or a plant. Write the project log page.

terms.title: Spring · Fire, Knife and Rope II, and Groundskeeping

head: Strands
Fire, Knife and Rope (§6): fire and whittling · Groundskeeping and Heavy Work (§6)
rows: Skills
The fire triangle and fire safety · gathering and sorting fuel · building and putting out a fire · cooking on a fire · whittling wood · wheelbarrow and shovel
Projects

Courtesy of the term
Walking on the street side
Tasks
A skill · B real work (2 a week × 6 = 12)

reference.title: Fire rules (teach in week 25, before any fire)

blocks.text: 1. A fire is built only with an adult, who lights it and stays with it the whole time.
2. Use a fire pit or a cleared ring of bare earth or stones, away from buildings, trees and dry grass. Check the weather: no fires on windy or dry days, and follow any local burn rules.
3. Have a bucket of water and a shovel ready before the first match.
4. Never leave a fire. Long hair tied back; loose sleeves rolled up.
5. Putting it out: drown it with water, stir the ashes, drown it again, and feel for heat with the back of your hand held above it. It's out only when it's cold.

reference.title: Courtesy of the term: walking on the street side

blocks.text: When walking with others on a sidewalk, walk on the side nearest the traffic. In the past, this protected others from splashes and runaway carts; today it still puts you between them and the road. At week 30, ask: when did you remember?

The fire triangle: a fire needs heat, fuel and air; take away any one and it goes out. (Science Term 4 showed a candle going out under a jar.) Then the fire rules, said back by the child. Choose and prepare the fire site with the adult.

Gather and sort fuel into three piles: tinder (dry grass, birch bark, wood shavings), kindling (sticks the thickness of a pencil), and fuel (sticks as thick as a wrist). Only dead, dry wood from the ground.

Building a fire lay. A teepee: a tinder bundle in the middle, kindling leaned around it in a cone, with a gap on the side the wind comes from. A log cabin: kindling stacked in squares around the tinder. The adult lights it; the child adds kindling, then fuel, slowly.
Build a small fire, watch it, and put it out following rule 5, until it's cold to the touch.
Cooking on a fire: wait until the flames die down to glowing coals; coals cook, flames burn. Hold food above the coals, not in the flames.
Cook a snack: bread twisted on a stick, a foil-wrapped potato, or a marshmallow. Then put the fire out completely. (A good one to do with the Hearth track.)

Whittling wood. Review the knife rules. Use a soft wood (a green stick, or a block of basswood). Sit with elbows on knees, the stick held to the side, and push the blade away from the body in short, shallow strokes, taking off thin curls.
Whittle a tent stake: a stick about 8 inches long, with a point at one end and a notch near the top for the rope.

Wheelbarrow and shovel. Load the wheelbarrow low and toward the front; lift with the legs, not the back; push, don't pull. With a shovel: foot on the blade, push it in, bend the knees, and lift small loads.
Clear and dig a garden bed: pull weeds, turn the soil, and work in compost. This is the kitchen garden bed for the Hearth track to plant (Hearth Term 5).
Tool care: clean the shovel and wheelbarrow; wipe and oil the knife blade and close it. Then the skills checklist (below).
Finish the garden bed, and write the project log page.

glance.text: Toward Grade 5. The outline's culminating Workshop work in Grade 5 includes "a documented home repair from diagnosis to finish" (§6). This term's repair is the first, small step.

reference.title: Courtesy of the term: greeting adults

blocks.text: When meeting an adult, stand up, look them in the eye, offer a firm (not crushing) handshake, and say "Good morning, Mr. ___" or "It's nice to meet you." Practice at home first. At week 36, ask: whom did you greet well?

Stacking wood. Build the ends of the pile in a crisscross ("log cabin") so they don't fall; lay the rest bark side up, off the ground on two rails or pallets, with a little space for air. If there's no firewood, practice with scrap lumber or bricks.
Stack a woodpile (or tidy a lumber pile) neatly.
Tidying the grounds: picking up fallen sticks, raking clippings, pulling weeds by the root, sweeping a path. Work from one end to the other so nothing is missed.
An afternoon of yard work with the family.

Finding a fault. Go back to the Term 3 house map and walk-round notes. Look and listen for small problems: a loose cabinet hinge, a squeaky door, a wobbly chair, a loose drawer knob, a nail hole in a wall. Choose one to fix.
Plan the repair with a parent: what's wrong, what tools are needed, and the steps. Write it on the repair page (below). Draw or photograph it before.

Small repairs: tightening a screw with the right screwdriver; tightening a loose hinge; quieting a squeaky hinge with a drop of oil; filling a small nail hole with spackle, smoothed with a putty knife and sanded when dry.
Do the repair, with the parent beside you.
Writing it up. A good repair record says what was wrong, how you found the cause, what you used, what you did, and how it works now.
Finish the repair page, with an after drawing or photo. It goes in the portfolio.

blocks.text: Small repairs, real results. A child who has fixed a squeaky door knows something is broken can be made right. That's the Workshop's whole point.
Keep the repair pages. By Grade 5 they make a record of everything the child has learned to fix.
